SOURCE: old lesson 24, 2,102 words, and the syllabus is explicit that only part of it belongs here -- old 24 was a futures-sizing lesson, and its Part 2 (margin is not risk) is slot 14's claim while its minimum-account arithmetic is slot 20's. What survived into this slot is the one thing that is a property of the OBJECT rather than of the account: a futures contract cannot be cut in half. Everything else here is new. WHAT THE SLOT IS FOR: slot 12 chose the instrument; this asks what kind of legal thing you would be holding, and answers it with four questions the object settles before you have an opinion -- the smallest position it permits, whether it expires, the most it can take, and who is obliged to pay you. The four objects are a share, a futures contract, an option and a perpetual, chosen because between them they cover the distinct combinations of those four columns. The sharpest cell is the share's last one: NOBODY owes you, which is why realising a share is exactly slot 12's friction problem and nobody else's obligation. The perpetual pays off slot 10's financing charge: it has no roll and a continuous funding payment instead, and it is the only one of the four whose charge changes sign. NUMBERS, all re-run in Python: S&P 500 at 5,000, so an ETF share is about $500, one MES controls 5,000 x $5 = $25,000 and one ES controls $250,000 -- the smallest position on the same index in the same direction spans a factor of 500. One option contract covers 100 ETF shares = $50,000 of exposure against a premium of 0.4 x 500 x 0.16 x sqrt(1/12) = $9.24 a share, $924 a contract, so exposure is 54x the outlay and the outlay is the whole loss. WHAT THE SLOT IS FOR: margin is collateral, not a loss measure, and the two numbers are set by different people for different reasons. The move that makes it computable rather than moralising: leverage is not a setting but a ratio, notional over equity, and from it one exact fact falls out -- at leverage L an adverse move of 1/L is the entire deposit. NUMBERS, all re-run in Python and each row cross-checked so that points x point value equals the deposit: MES at S&P 5,000 is $25,000 notional; $25,000 equity is 1x and needs 100% (5,000 points), $2,500 is 10x and needs 10% (500 points), $500 is 50x and needs 2% (100 points). Against that, a ten-point stop risks $50 -- 2% of a $2,500 deposit and 0.2% of notional, so the margin is 50x the risk and neither number tells you the other.
